title: Prehistoric Northwest Arabia
subtitle: 8,000–1,200 BC · Mustatils, the Funerary Avenues and the Walled Oases of Tayma and Khaybar

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No king-lists survive — the record runs from the return of the herders, through the great ritual-building horizon, to the walled Bronze Age oasis towns

entries.label: Herders return to the Hejaz and Najd margins
entries.loc: the Nefud margins and the Harrat volcanic fields, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: As the early Holocene monsoon pushed rain deeper into the Arabian interior, cattle-, sheep- and goat-herding groups spread out from the Nefud margins into the Hejaz and the Harrat lava fields — the population that would, in a few thousand years, build the mustatils and the kites.
entries.note: Hatton, Guagnin, Petraglia, Groucutt et al., landscape surveys of the Neolithic Nefud margin, summarised in 'Landscape positioning of Neolithic mustatil stone structures...', Holocene (2024). Cross-references the Holocene Humid Period entry in gulf-prehistory-8000bc-3000bc.

entries.label: Jubbah — a lakeside gathering place
entries.hint: Jubbah's freshwater lake, fed by the same humid phase, drew Neolithic herders back again and again; its shores carry one of the densest concentrations of prehistoric rock art anywhere in Arabia and later became a UNESCO World Heritage landscape for exactly that reason.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., 'Rock art imagery as a proxy for Holocene environmental change: a view from Shuwaymis, Saudi Arabia', Holocene (2015) and related Jubbah survey publications.

entries.label: The Camel Site community, Sakaka
entries.loc: near Sakaka, al-Jawf Province, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: At a single rock outcrop near Sakaka, a Neolithic community carved, and repeatedly recarved over generations, twelve life-sized reliefs of camels and equids — a fixed gathering place contemporary with the mustatil-building horizon, contact for grooves marking each new season's visit.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., 'Life-sized Neolithic camel sculptures in Arabia: a scientific assessment of the craftsmanship and age of the Camel Site reliefs', Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports (2022).

entries.label: The mustatil-building horizon
entries.hint: Over a period of a few centuries, herding communities across northwestern Arabia built more than 1,600 low-walled rectangular stone monuments — the mustatils — the first large-scale, non-domestic construction tradition in the peninsula, predating the pyramids and Stonehenge by a wide margin.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., 'The mustatils: cult and monumentality in Neolithic north-western Arabia', Antiquity (2021); Hatton et al., Holocene (2024), for the revised radiocarbon range (5400–4200 BC).

entries.group: The Bronze Age Oasis Towns (2600–1200 BC)
entries.label: Tayma's walled oasis begins
entries.hint: An 18.2-kilometre stone wall enclosing roughly 1,000 hectares around the Tayma oasis was begun in the third millennium BC and expanded in the early second — one of the largest Bronze Age fortifications documented anywhere in Arabia, built to manage a seasonal oasis rather than a dense city.
entries.note: the Saudi-German Tayma Project (German Archaeological Institute and the Saudi Heritage Commission), OSL and stratigraphic dating summarised in Hausleiter, 'Ancient Tayma — an Oasis at the interface between cultures', in Franke (ed.), Roads of Arabia (2011), and subsequent project reports.

entries.group: The Bronze Age Oasis Towns (2600–1200 BC)
entries.label: Al-Natah, the walled town of Khaybar
entries.loc: Khaybar oasis, Medina Province, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: A fortified 2.6-hectare town of about 500 people, with roughly 50 uniform houses, a residential quarter, an administrative quarter and a stepped-tomb necropolis, ringed by a 14.5-kilometre rampart — the first recorded example of Bronze Age town planning in northwest Arabia. It was abandoned, for reasons still unclear, around 1300–1500 BC.
entries.note: Charloux et al., 'A Bronze Age town in the Khaybar walled oasis: debating early urbanization in Northwestern Arabia', PLOS ONE (2024) — announced by the CNRS and the Royal Commission for AlUla in February 2024.

entries.group: The Bronze Age Oasis Towns (2600–1200 BC)
entries.label: Qurayyah — the painted-pottery centre
entries.hint: By the very end of this folio's span, the oasis of Qurayyah had become the production centre for a distinctive geometric painted pottery — long called 'Midianite ware' after the biblical Midianites, now generally termed Qurayyah Painted Ware — that circulated as far as the Egyptian-run copper mines of the southern Levant.
entries.note: the ware's dating is debated: conventionally 13th–12th century BC on Egyptian associations at Timna, though some scholars argue for a longer use-life into the Iron Age. See Rothenberg and Glass, and the review in Tebes (ed.), Unearthing the Wilderness (2014).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Only two things look like organised violence in this record: the walls people built, and the collapse of the town those walls were built to protect

entries.label: Tayma's and Al-Natah's walls as a response to instability
entries.hint: Both excavation teams read their oasis walls as defensive rather than purely administrative — Al-Natah's 14.5 km rampart and Tayma's 18.2 km enclosure suggest endemic low-level raiding on settled, resource-rich oases by the surrounding mobile population, rather than warfare against a named rival state.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024); the Tayma Project's own reports frame the wall similarly. No named enemy or battle is recorded — the inference is architectural, from the scale and placement of the fortifications.

entries.label: Al-Natah is abandoned
entries.hint: Al-Natah's excavators cannot yet say why the town emptied — climate stress, the same resource pressures that were destabilising urban systems from Mycenaean Greece to the Hittite kingdom by 1200 BC, or a purely local cause. Its abandonment sits at the edge of, and may or may not connect to, the wider Late Bronze Age crisis.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024), state the cause of abandonment as an open question; the possible link to the broader c.1200 BC Eastern Mediterranean collapse is this folio's own speculative framing, not a claim made in the excavation report.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Ritual monuments and funerary corridors, not palaces, are the visible infrastructure of social organisation in this era

entries.label: Mustatils as a claim on kinship and territory
entries.hint: Interpreted by their excavators as votive rather than funerary or domestic, the mustatils are read as communal infrastructure — built by many hands, used to construct and repeatedly reaffirm kinship ties and a shared social identity across dispersed pastoral groups, and to mark territory in a landscape without permanent settlement.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021); Kennedy, Thomas et al., 'The nexus of cult and pastoralism in Neolithic Northwest Arabia', Open Quaternary (2024).

entries.label: The betyl and the horn deposit inside the mustatil
entries.hint: Inside many mustatil chambers, excavators found a standing stone (a betyl) surrounded by hundreds of cattle, sheep, goat and gazelle horns — a repeated votive act, plausibly for rain, herd fertility or flock health, performed by the same community across generations rather than a single dedication.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021), on the excavated chamber at IDIHA-0008.

entries.label: The funerary avenues as connective infrastructure
entries.loc: between Khaybar, AlUla and Tayma, northwest Arabia
entries.hint: A network of long pathways, lined on both sides with tombs and traceable across some 160,000 km2, linked the major oases and the water sources between them — more than 17,800 'pendant' tombs have been recorded in the AlUla survey area alone, evidence that pastoral groups across a huge area were part of one connected social and territorial system.
entries.note: Dalton et al., 'The Middle Holocene 'funerary avenues' of north-west Arabia', The Holocene (2022); fieldwork by the University of Western Australia for the Royal Commission for AlUla.

entries.label: Tayma's oasis-scale governance
entries.hint: A walled area of roughly 1,000 hectares vastly exceeds anything the resident population needed for housing alone; the excavators read it as infrastructure for managing seasonal pastoral influx, caravan traffic and the oasis's water and date-palm gardens — governance of a resource, not just a settlement.
entries.note: Hausleiter, in Franke (ed.), Roads of Arabia (2011); the Tayma Project's ongoing reports on the oasis wall system.

entries.label: Al-Natah's zoned town plan
entries.hint: For the first time in northwest Arabia, a settlement is laid out in distinct functional zones — a residential quarter of roughly fifty uniform houses, a separate administrative quarter, and a necropolis of stepped tower-tombs — a deliberate, if small-scale, act of town planning rather than organic accretion.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A votive, herd-centred cult built around standing stones — the earliest phase of a betyl tradition that runs, arguably, all the way to the Nabataean baetyls of the following millennia

entries.label: The Camel Site as a seasonal gathering ritual
entries.hint: The Camel Site reliefs were not carved once and left; they were repeatedly retouched, regrooved and modified over what may be generations, implying the site drew the same community back on a recurring, probably seasonal, basis — closer to a place of pilgrimage than a single monument.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports (2022).

entries.label: The mustatil votive cult
entries.hint: Hundreds of horns placed around a standing stone, repeated at site after site, describe a shared ritual grammar across a huge area of the Neolithic Hejaz: an appeal, most plausibly, for rain, fertile herds and healthy flocks, performed communally rather than by an individual priest or ruler.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021); Thomas, Kennedy et al., Open Quaternary (2024).

entries.label: The betyl — a standing-stone tradition with a long afterlife
entries.hint: The aniconic standing stone at the heart of the mustatil cult is the earliest dated example of a practice — worship focused on an unworked or minimally worked stone rather than a carved image — that recurs across pre-Islamic Arabia for millennia, including in the Nabataean religion many centuries later.
entries.note: the long continuity of betyl worship in Arabia is a standard observation in Nabataean religious studies (e.g. Healey, 'The Religion of the Nabataeans', 2001); the mustatil evidence pushes its earliest secure archaeological anchor back to the Neolithic. Flagged as a candidate cross-reference to the Nabataean folio's own betyl material.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Two entirely different monumental traditions — figurative rock relief and abstract dry-stone architecture — appear within a few centuries of each other and nowhere else in the world at this date

entries.label: The rock art of Jubbah
entries.hint: Thousands of engraved panels around Jubbah's former lake record herding, hunting and human figures across millennia of continuous use, from Neolithic pastoralists through later periods — dense enough, and well enough preserved, that UNESCO inscribed the Hail rock art landscape (Jubbah and Shuwaymis) as a World Heritage site in 2015.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., 'Rock art imagery as a proxy for Holocene environmental change', Holocene (2015); UNESCO World Heritage listing, 'Rock Art in the Hail Region of Saudi Arabia' (2015).

entries.label: The Camel Site reliefs
entries.hint: Twelve surviving reliefs, carved with stone tools out of a sandstone outcrop, depict at least ten camels and three equids at life size — a scale and naturalism unmatched by any other Near Eastern rock art of comparable age, misdated on discovery to the Nabataean period until re-analysis of tool marks and weathering placed it firmly in the Neolithic.
entries.note: Guagnin et al., Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports (2022); the initial 2018 misdating to c.2,000 years old is itself a documented case study in monument dating method.

entries.label: The mustatils — monumental architecture before writing
entries.hint: Ranging from 20 metres to more than 600 metres long, the mustatils are the oldest large-scale stone monuments yet dated anywhere on the Arabian Peninsula, predating both Stonehenge (c.3000 BC) and the Giza pyramids (c.2560 BC) by well over a thousand years — built by herding communities with no writing, no metal and, so far as is known, no rulers.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021).

entries.label: Tayma's Bronze Age wall
entries.hint: At 18.2 kilometres long, enclosing roughly 1,000 hectares, Tayma's oasis wall is among the largest single Bronze Age construction projects documented in Arabia — built and expanded in stone, without the state bureaucracy that produced comparably scaled fortifications in contemporary Mesopotamia or Egypt.
entries.note: the Saudi-German Tayma Project; Hausleiter, in Franke (ed.), Roads of Arabia (2011).

entries.label: The stepped tower-tombs of Al-Natah
entries.hint: Al-Natah's necropolis holds tower-tombs built up in visible steps — a distinct funerary architecture from the pendant tombs lining the funerary avenues nearby, suggesting the settled townspeople of Khaybar marked death differently from the mobile pastoral groups whose tombs line the roads between the oases.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024).

entries.label: Qurayyah Painted Ware
entries.hint: Fine buff-ware vessels decorated in geometric red-and-black bands and stylised birds, produced at Qurayyah and traded widely, are the most visually distinctive craft object of Late Bronze Age northwest Arabia and the clearest single marker of the oasis network's reach beyond the peninsula.
entries.note: Rothenberg and Glass's original 'Midianite pottery' studies; the current 'Qurayyah Painted Ware' terminology and its debated chronology are reviewed in Tebes (ed.), Unearthing the Wilderness (2014).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Landscape-scale remote sensing, radiocarbon dating and zooarchaeology are how this era is known at all — there is no written word from it

entries.label: Reading Tayma's ancient shoreline
entries.hint: The high-water marks of Tayma's vanished Holocene lake are still visible well up the basin sides; matching their elevation against the modern water balance implies rainfall several times higher than today during the oasis's formative centuries — a paleoclimate reading made from landform alone, without a single datable object.
entries.note: the Saudi-German Tayma Project's geomorphological survey work, part of the wider project reported in Hausleiter (2011) and subsequent seasons.

entries.label: Satellite and helicopter survey reveal a hidden landscape
entries.hint: The mustatils and the funerary avenues were both found the same way: satellite imagery flagged anomalous linear and rectangular features across tens of thousands of square kilometres, which helicopter-based aerial photography and then ground survey confirmed and dated — archaeology conducted at a landscape scale that no ground survey alone could have achieved.
entries.note: the AAKSA (Aerial Archaeology in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia) project, University of Western Australia and the Royal Commission for AlUla; methodology set out in Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021) and Dalton et al., The Holocene (2022).

entries.label: Radiocarbon and OSL fix the mustatil chronology
entries.hint: Fewer than a dozen of the more than 1,600 mapped mustatils have been excavated, but radiocarbon dates from those few narrowed the building horizon to roughly 5400–4200 BC — a chronology repeatedly revised as new excavations and reassessed samples came in.
entries.note: Hatton et al., The Holocene (2024), superseding the wider date ranges proposed in the original 2021 Antiquity paper.

entries.label: Horn counts as an economic archive
entries.hint: Zooarchaeological identification of the hundreds of horn cores deposited inside excavated mustatils — sorted by species (cattle, sheep, goat, gazelle) and, where possible, by age and sex — reconstructs the herd management and hunting practices of a community that left no other economic record at all.
entries.note: the zooarchaeological analysis in Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: A pastoral economy that grows, at its two richest oases, into managed date-palm agriculture and long-distance trade — while the interior stays overwhelmingly a herder's world

entries.label: Tayma's lake and a much wetter oasis
entries.hint: The elevation of Tayma's fossil shorelines implies rainfall roughly three times the modern level during the formative Holocene — the wet backdrop against which the oasis's earliest settlement and, eventually, its Bronze Age wall were built.
entries.note: Tayma Project geomorphological survey, in Hausleiter (2011) and later seasons.

entries.label: Cattle, sheep and goat pastoralism becomes dominant
entries.hint: The horn deposits inside the mustatils are overwhelmingly domestic cattle, sheep and goat rather than wild gazelle — direct evidence that herding, not hunting, had become the economic base of the communities that built and used them.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021), zooarchaeological report.

entries.label: Oasis agriculture at Tayma and Khaybar
entries.hint: Both walled oases combined date-palm cultivation and irrigated grain farming with continued herding and trade — a mixed, flexible subsistence base the Al-Natah excavators call 'low urbanization', deliberately resilient to an unpredictable, fluctuating rainfall regime rather than betting everything on a single mode of production.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024).

entries.label: The funerary avenues double as trade corridors
entries.hint: The same avenues that carried the dead to their tombs also connected the major oases and their water sources — the excavators argue the populations of Bronze Age northwest Arabia were far more economically and socially interconnected across long distances than previously assumed.
entries.note: Dalton et al., The Holocene (2022).

entries.label: Qurayyah ware reaches the Levantine copper mines
entries.hint: Qurayyah Painted Ware turns up at Timna in the Negev, at a copper-smelting site operated under Egyptian New Kingdom authority — physical evidence that Hejazi oasis communities were trading (or moving) as far as the Levantine copper industry that supplied Late Bronze Age Egypt.
entries.note: Rothenberg and Glass's Timna reports; the trade-versus-migration interpretation of the ware's presence at Timna is still debated (Tebes, 2014).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Dry-stone construction at landscape scale, coordinated hunting architecture and a distinctive painted ceramic tradition

entries.label: The kite complexes of the Harrat
entries.loc: the Harrat volcanic fields near Khaybar and AlUla
entries.hint: Long converging stone walls, funnelling toward a pit or enclosure, still cover the lava fields east of Khaybar and AlUla — a mass-hunting technology for driving and trapping gazelle herds, built by the same pastoral communities responsible for the mustatils, in a tradition also documented on the Gulf coast far to the east.
entries.note: kite research across northern Arabia is summarised in Kennedy, 'Kites: new discoveries and a new type', Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy (2012). Cross-references the desert-kite entry in the gulf-prehistory folio, a parallel but geographically distinct kite tradition.

entries.label: Dry-stone construction at monumental scale
entries.hint: The mustatils were built without mortar, in low double walls sometimes exceeding 600 metres in length, using locally quarried stone — a construction method requiring no metal tools and no central authority, only sustained, organised communal labour repeated at more than 1,600 separate locations.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021).

entries.label: Tayma's fortification and water engineering
entries.hint: An 18.2 km stone wall, built and later extended without mortar, enclosed the oasis's wells and gardens alongside its settlement — construction on a scale that required organising labour across a wide, low-density population over multiple building phases.
entries.note: the Saudi-German Tayma Project reports.

entries.label: Al-Natah's rampart and street grid
entries.hint: A 14.5 km rampart and an internally organised street layout at Al-Natah show deliberate town-planning technique applied at a small scale — engineering know-how transplanted from the region's larger oasis-wall tradition (as at Tayma) to a settlement of only a few hundred people.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024).

entries.label: Qurayyah's ceramic technique
entries.hint: Qurayyah's potters worked a fine buff clay fabric and a controlled, even firing to support crisp painted geometric decoration — a specialised production technology distinct from the coarser domestic wares used elsewhere in the same oasis network.
entries.note: Rothenberg and Glass; the fabric analysis is summarised in Tebes (ed.), Unearthing the Wilderness (2014).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A local network of oases and avenues that, by the very end of this folio, plugs into trade routes reaching the Egyptian-run mines of the southern Levant

entries.label: A Neolithic reprise of Arabia as a corridor
entries.hint: The same humid-phase pattern that let Palaeolithic hominins move through Arabia now let Neolithic herders spread across the whole interior — a much shorter-range, much better-evidenced version of the same climate-driven corridor effect, this time producing monuments rather than footprints.
entries.note: synthesis observation, following the framing common to Kennedy et al. (2021) and the broader Green Arabia literature.

entries.label: The funerary avenues as northwest Arabia's own road network
entries.hint: Long before the classical incense route ran through the same landscape, the funerary avenues already linked its major water sources and oases across some 160,000 km2 — the deep prehistoric ancestor of the caravan geography that later carried frankincense and myrrh through exactly this corridor.
entries.note: Dalton et al., The Holocene (2022); the later incense-route geography is treated in the Nabataean folio.

entries.label: A shared building tradition across the oases
entries.hint: Tayma and Al-Natah were built using the same walled-oasis method — massive dry-stone enclosure, an internal zoned settlement, a stepped-tomb necropolis — evidence the two towns, though founded independently and roughly 130 km apart, belonged to one shared regional culture rather than two coincidentally similar ones.
entries.note: the parallel is drawn explicitly in the Charloux et al. (2024) discussion of Al-Natah against the published Tayma material.

entries.label: Qurayyah ware and contact with New Kingdom Egypt's mining frontier
entries.hint: Whether carried by trade, by the movement of specialist potters, or by the Hejazi population later remembered in the biblical record as Midianites, Qurayyah ware's presence at an Egyptian-administered copper mine is the clearest evidence of northwest Arabia's contact with the wider Late Bronze Age Near Eastern world.
entries.note: Rothenberg's original Timna excavation reports; the population/trade question is unresolved (Tebes, 2014).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A 'lost' network civilization comes into view — one that answered the challenge of an unstable climate with mobility and ritual infrastructure rather than a single dense city

entries.label: A previously unrecognised Arabian network civilization
entries.hint: Taken together, the mustatils, the funerary avenues and the walled oases of Tayma and Al-Natah describe a genuinely new picture: a connected, ritually and economically integrated society across the Hejaz and Najd interior, invisible until 21st-century remote sensing revealed its scale.
entries.note: the synthesis is the field's own — see Kennedy et al. (2021), Dalton et al. (2022) and Charloux et al. (2024) each explicitly situating their find within this larger emerging picture.

entries.label: 'Low urbanization' as an alternative answer to instability
entries.hint: While contemporary Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Levant built dense, permanent cities, the Hejaz answered the same Bronze Age challenges — surplus, defence, water management — with flexible, low-density 'slow urbanism': walled but sparsely built oases that could contract or expand with an unpredictable climate rather than committing to permanent density.
entries.note: 'low urbanization' and 'slow urbanism' are the excavators' own terms — Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024). A deliberate historiographic corrective to reading non-dense settlement as evidence of a lesser civilization.

entries.label: Tayma's rainfall crash
entries.hint: The high Holocene shorelines at Tayma had no modern successor: rainfall three times today's level did not persist, and the oasis's Bronze Age wall was ultimately built and maintained under a drying climate, not a wet one — a slow environmental contraction running underneath this folio's whole political and architectural story.
entries.note: Tayma Project geomorphological survey, Hausleiter (2011) and later seasons.

entries.label: An open question: does the c.1200 BC crisis reach the Hejaz?
entries.hint: Al-Natah's abandonment and the very end of secure dating for the funerary-avenue network both fall close to the wider Late Bronze Age collapse that unseated the Hittite kingdom and the Mycenaean palaces further north — whether northwest Arabia felt the same systemic shock, or simply reached the end of its own separate trajectory at the same time, is not yet answered.
entries.note: genuinely unresolved; framed here as an open question rather than an established connection, since no publication has yet argued the link directly.

entries.label: The thread continues — Dadan, Lihyan and the Nabataeans
entries.hint: This folio stops at 1200 BC because its evidence runs out here, not because the region's history does: the oasis of Dadan (modern AlUla) becomes, from around the mid-first millennium BC, the seat of the Dadanite and then Lihyanite kingdoms, and the same corridor is carrying the incense trade by the time the Nabataean kingdom — already covered in its own folio — takes shape at Petra.
entries.note: a forward reference, not yet built: a Dadan-and-Lihyan folio (region 'Arabia', c.1000–100 BC) would bridge the gap to nabataean-312bc-106ce.json, which already covers this folio's eventual successor state.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Thousands of unnamed builders and thousands of unnamed tombs are the real population of this folio — Al-Natah's few hundred residents are the closest thing to a named community

entries.label: The pastoral majority, mostly invisible
entries.hint: Most people in this world were never settled at all — pastoralists moving between the oases and the Harrat, whose material trace is a scatter of tombs along a funerary avenue or a horn deposit in a mustatil, not a house floor. The walled towns this folio can describe in detail were always the exception, not the rule.
entries.note: a framing observation, following the same 'reject the empty-desert narrative' caution the project applies to the Gulf folios — here directed at over-weighting the excavated towns relative to the far larger mobile population the surveys imply.

entries.label: The mustatil builders
entries.hint: More than 1,600 monuments, most requiring substantial coordinated labour, were built by communities that erected no monument to any individual within them — the builders are visible only as an aggregate, generation after generation performing the same votive act at the same kind of structure.
entries.note: Kennedy et al., Antiquity (2021).

entries.label: Seventeen thousand marked, unnamed graves
entries.loc: along the funerary avenues, northwest Arabia
entries.hint: More than 17,800 pendant tombs line the AlUla survey area's avenues alone — each one a deliberate, visible act of commemoration for a specific person, and every one of those people now entirely anonymous. The avenues preserve the fact of individual lives and deaths at a scale almost no other prehistoric society records, without preserving a single name.
entries.note: Dalton et al., The Holocene (2022).

entries.label: The five hundred of Al-Natah
entries.hint: Roughly fifty near-identical houses across Al-Natah's residential quarter imply a population of some 500 people living without the marked wealth differences visible at larger contemporary cities — an unusually egalitarian material record, at least at the level the excavated houses can show.
entries.note: Charloux et al., PLOS ONE (2024).
